Multiple agents on one WhatsApp number: how to end the chaos

Two agents replying to the same customer while another customer gets no reply at all are usually the same problem. And hiring more people won't fix it.

LVBy Lucas Vaz·October 16, 2026·7 min read

Key takeaways

  • The chaos doesn't come from message volume; it comes from conversations with no owner.
  • Pick one routing rule: a single queue, by department or by customer account.
  • Every transfer carries an internal note so the customer never repeats their story.
  • A five-minute shift handover prevents most forgotten conversations.
  • Define roles: who answers, who supervises and who changes settings.

Monday, 10 a.m., at a building supply store. Three salespeople answer the same WhatsApp number. A customer asks the price of porcelain tile. Two reply at the same time with different prices, because one checked the new price list and the other the old one. Meanwhile, a customer who asked about Friday's delivery has been waiting since 8 a.m. Each salesperson assumed someone else would answer.

Having multiple agents on one WhatsApp number is a natural step for any growing business. The chaos that often comes with it isn't natural. It has a cause, and the cause is almost always the same: conversations with no owner.

If your main problem is slow replies, start with how to answer WhatsApp customers faster. This piece covers something else: how to organize the team so everyone can work on the same number without stepping on each other.

Signs your shared number has turned into a mess

Count how many of these happen in your business:

  • Two people reply to the same customer, sometimes with different information.
  • A customer gets no reply because the message was read and nobody took it.
  • The company phone gets passed around and disappears at the end of the day.
  • Nobody can say who promised what: "who said we'd deliver tomorrow?"
  • When someone goes on vacation, their conversations just sit there.
  • The customer has to repeat everything when they're passed to another agent.

Two or more of these and the cost is already real. Try a hypothetical: if a business gets 60 conversations a day and 5% are forgotten, that's three customers a day with no reply, about 65 a month over 22 working days. If one in five was going to buy, that's 13 sales vanishing without anyone noticing.

What are the options for several agents on one number?

There are basically three paths. Each works at some team size; the trouble starts when you use the wrong one for yours.

OptionWorks forWhere it breaks
One shared phone1 person, low volumeOnly one can reply at a time; the phone is the bottleneck
Business app with linked devices2 or 3 peopleEveryone sees everything; no owner, no routing
Platform on the official APITeams of any sizePlatform cost plus Meta's fees

The WhatsApp Business app lets you use the same account on other devices. The WhatsApp Help Center mentions up to four linked devices at a time. For two or three people with an agreed routine, that's enough. What the app doesn't do is tell you who is handling each conversation. Everyone sees everything, and in practice "everyone" becomes "no one."

On the official API, each agent signs in with their own login to a shared inbox, and the customer still sees a single number. The difference between the two is explained in WhatsApp Business app vs API.

How to route conversations between agents

Once you have the right tool, you need the rule. There are three main routing models, and most businesses use one of them or a mix of two.

ModelHow it worksGood for
Single queueWhoever is free takes the next chatSimilar questions, small team
By departmentSales, billing and support have their own queuesVery different topics
By accountEach customer has a fixed agentRepeat buyers, long relationships

A pizzeria with three people on a Saturday night does fine with a single queue: everyone can answer about the menu and delivery. A clinic usually separates scheduling from billing, because whoever books appointments shouldn't be handling refunds. A real estate agency or a distributor serving retailers leans toward accounts: the customer wants to talk to "their" agent or rep.

With accounts, always name a backup. A rep's day off can't mean a customer with no reply.

The rule that fixes half the problems: every conversation has an owner

Write this on a sheet of paper and stick it on the wall: whoever claims it, answers it. If you didn't claim it, you don't answer.

In practice, it works like this:

  1. A new conversation arrives. It sits in the "unassigned" list.
  2. Someone claims it (or the routing rule assigns it) before typing a single word.
  3. From then on, only the owner replies. Others can read, but they don't jump in.
  4. If the owner can't continue, they transfer it. They don't abandon it.

It sounds rigid. It's what ends double replies and forgotten customers in one move. And there's a bonus: when a customer complains, you know who to talk to.

Introducing yourself when you take over helps too, especially when the customer has already spoken with someone else:

Hi Carla! This is Diego, I'll be looking after your order from here. I see you need the 24x24 porcelain tile by Friday. Let me check stock and I'll send you the price with delivery.

How to transfer without the customer repeating everything

The transfer is where most customers get lost. The new agent arrives with no context, asks again what the customer already explained, and patience runs out.

The fix is an internal note, visible only to the team, written before the transfer. Always use the same three points:

What the customer wants: gray 24x24 porcelain tile, 450 sq ft, delivery to the north side.
What's been done: sent the price per sq ft; they asked for a cash discount.
What's left: get the discount approved by the manager and confirm Friday delivery.

It takes thirty seconds and saves five minutes of back-and-forth. If your tool has no internal notes, agree on a format in the team group chat with the customer's number at the start of the message. It's worse, but better than nothing.

The same logic applies when the AI hands over to a person: whoever takes over needs a summary, not a "good luck." The criteria for deciding when AI answers and when it calls someone are in AI or human agent: when to hand off.

Shift handover: the five minutes that prevent forgotten chats

A lot of conversations die at shift change. The morning agent promised to get back "this afternoon" and went home. The afternoon agent doesn't know about the promise.

A short handover, always at the same time, solves it. Copy this routine:

Weekends and holidays deserve an on-call plan in writing: who covers, until what time, and what waits until Monday.

Roles and permissions: who can do what

Once the team grows past three or four people, not everyone needs to see and change everything. Three roles cover most cases:

  • Agent: claims, answers and transfers conversations in their queue or account list.
  • Supervisor: sees all queues, reassigns stalled conversations and tracks team numbers.
  • Admin: connects numbers and changes settings, the AI and campaigns.

A separate admin role prevents the classic "someone changed the away message and nobody knows who." Separating departments also protects information: the sales intern doesn't need to see a customer's conversation about an overdue invoice.

Start with one rule, tomorrow morning

Don't try to roll out everything at once. Tomorrow, before you open, gather the team for five minutes and agree on just this: nobody answers a conversation without claiming it first.

Let it run for a week. You'll see double replies disappear almost immediately, and the "unassigned" list will show, for the first time, how many conversations used to sit in limbo. The following week, add the transfer note. Then the shift handover.

Three simple rules, one per week. Within a month the shared number stops being a problem and becomes what it should have been from the start: the place where the whole team talks to customers without tripping over each other.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use the same WhatsApp number on several phones?

The WhatsApp Business app lets you link a few devices to the same account, but with no chat assignment or owner. For larger teams, the path is a platform on the official API, where each agent signs in with their own login.

How do I stop two agents from answering the same customer?

Make it a rule that every conversation has an owner and only the owner replies. Whoever picks up a new conversation claims it before typing. Transfers go through the tool with a note, not by shouting across the room.

What's the best way to route conversations between agents?

It depends on the business. A single queue works for similar questions and small teams; by department when topics are very different; by account when customers buy again and the relationship matters.

Will customers notice they're talking to different people?

Only if the handover is sloppy. With visible history and an internal note, whoever takes over picks up where things left off. Still, introducing yourself by name when you take over is a courtesy customers appreciate.
